content.title: Do Christians and Muslims mean the same thing by Jesus?
content.summary: Shared names do not remove the decisive question of his identity.

answer.text: There is overlap in vocabulary, but a decisive disagreement. Christianity confesses Jesus as the eternal Son, truly God and truly man. Qur'an 4:171 calls him Messiah and messenger while rejecting the language of three and God's having a son. Honour for Jesus as a messenger is not the same confession as worship of the incarnate Son.

reasoning.text: John identifies the Word as God and says that the Word became flesh.
Qur'an 4:171 places its statements about Jesus within an explicit rejection of divine sonship.
Thomas's confession to Jesus as Lord and God shows why the difference is substantive.

conclusion.text: We should explain the actual disagreement honestly while treating a Muslim neighbour with gentleness and respect.

sections.text: The Christian claim concerns the Son's eternal relation to the Father, not God producing a child by a sexual act. The incarnation is the eternal Son taking human nature. Distinguish these claims before answering an objection.
sections.title: Sonship is not biological procreation

sections.text: Read John 1 and Qur'an 4:171 in full. Do not turn the Qur'an's references to Jesus as a word or spirit into an admission of Nicene theology; the passage states its own boundaries. Ask your neighbour how they understand the text.
sections.title: Read each text in its own voice

content.objection: Isn't calling Jesus a great prophet enough?

reply.text: It does not match the Gospel's presentation of his identity. Jesus says the Son is to receive the honour given to the Father; Christian faith centres on who he is and what he accomplished.

limit.text: A primary text establishes a teaching to discuss; it does not tell you everything a particular Muslim believes. Let the person explain their own understanding.

prompt.text: What do you understand Christians to mean by Son of God, and could we compare that with John's account?
